h4: The Importance of a Strong Foundation
p: When the pandemic disrupted in-person visits to Starbucks' Coffee Farm visitor center in Costa Rica, our challenge was to create an immersive online alternative accessible from anywhere in the world.

Collaborating with Matterport, renowned for its 3D space technology, we tailored their platform to craft a virtual journey through Hacienda Alsacia. Led by a dedicated team, we aimed to capture the essence of Starbucks' coffee journey, from soil to cup, while aligning with their branding and Hacienda Alsacia's personality.
Through research, innovative design, and trust-building prototypes, we transformed adversity into an opportunity to bring Starbucks' coffee craftsmanship closer to partners and customers alike.
Help local merchants boost their sales during the pandemic while providing customers a way to save more money when shopping.
Conduct a comprehensive feasibility analysis to assess the market potential and viability of Nobolso as a sustainable cashback platform.
In early discovery workshops I had facilitated, some outstanding questions emerged from the team:
How could we attract merchants to perceive value and extract real benefits by joining this platform?
How can we encourage consumers to shop from these merchants via our platform? What's the incentive for someone to join?
Is this a feasible business venture?

To better understand these questions, we started with a consumer survey to see how often people use platforms like ours. Because of COVID-19, we talked to some of these users on WhatsApp. By looking at our competition and using our earlier research, we got more ideas and started designing the first versions of the consumer app.

Talking to merchants was very helpful. We found that convincing them to work with a platform like ours isn't easy. They had concerns like technical issues, worries about more competition, and how much discount they could give. Using this information and a Lean Business Canvas, we changed our approach later on.
We wanted to find out how people use other cashback platforms. Our survey revealed that one service was very popular because they gave cashback at gas stations.
By far, AME was the most used platform
After a workshop and crafting a Lean Business Canvas with stakeholders, I learned our main edge was a deal with the trading federation, giving us a large starting customer base.
Our biggest strength was based on a fragile deal.

I spoke to some of these users on WhatsApp. I learned that one platform did a lot of advertising at gas stations. With high gas prices, this got people's attention. It made us wonder: what could our service focus on to attract more users?
AME was popular because they provided discounts on gas stations

When I looked at other platforms, I noticed they all had their own strategies. Some targeted online shoppers, some focused on grocery store deals, and others wanted to be a digital wallet with special discounts.
This summary gave us a clearer view of our competition
After collecting the data and considering stakeholder strategies, I created the initial design for Nobolso. It's a cashback platform with an app for local deals and a website for merchant insights.

During interviews with local merchants, I discovered challenges our stakeholders hadn't initially considered. These included technical issues and concerns about competition on our platform. This suggested that getting merchants on board might take longer than expected. While merchants liked our customer insights feature, our small user base was a drawback.

We had hoped to gain access to a large 1.2 million user base by partnering with the local trading federation, but that deal didn't come through. After reviewing our findings, the stakeholders decided to stop the project since they felt the business wouldn't grow quickly enough.
My journey through this project provided several key insights.

Engaging in early product discovery can prevent unnecessary resource expenditure. Interviewing potential users and partners can bring essential insights to light, challenging stakeholder assumptions and aiding in informed decisions.
The COVID-19 pandemic necessitated adapting research methods. Using WhatsApp for qualitative research was effective and allowed for more extensive engagement than initially anticipated.

It's crucial to have a strong and reliable value proposition for any business. Factors external to the business can change the effectiveness of a perceived value proposition, and it's essential to regularly validate it.

Assumptions, especially those involving partnerships (like with the trading federation), can drastically affect outcomes. It's essential to ensure these foundational elements are solidified to prevent unexpected negative impacts.

p: The challenge was to automate the pick-and-place task, ensuring accurate object positioning and precise orientation in a simulated environment, which is essential for effective robotic manipulation.

To achieve this, YOLO was first used for object detection, providing bounding box coordinates for the detected objects. These coordinates were then combined with additional data from the simulation, such as object position and quaternion orientation, to build a comprehensive understanding of each object's location. Custom AI models were developed, with an XYZ model for spatial positioning and a YAW model for orientation control. Additionally, PID control was integrated to fine-tune the robot's movements, ensuring smooth and accurate task execution.
This simulation demonstrated the potential for a more efficient and accurate pick-and-place process, highlighting the capabilities of robotics automation in controlled environments.
Demonstrate the potential of robotics automation in a controlled simulation environment to automate repetitive tasks, reducing human error and increasing efficiency.
Improve the accuracy of object positioning and orientation in a pick-and-place task through custom AI models (XYZ for spatial positioning and YAW for orientation).
During the early phases of the project, several important questions emerged regarding the pick-and-place task and the integration of AI models:
How can we improve the accuracy of object detection and positioning in a robotic simulation?
What is the most effective way to combine AI-driven models (XYZ for positioning, YAW for orientation) with object detection data to ensure precise manipulation?
How can this simulation be used as a foundation for real-world robotics applications in manufacturing?

To address these questions, a systematic approach was taken to develop the pick-and-place simulation. This process involved integrating multiple techniques, each aimed at improving different aspects of robotic manipulation, such as object detection, positioning, and control. The approach was divided into four key steps:

The project began with data collection, combining real-world images of objects like cereal boxes, soda cans, and milk cartons with simulation data from the RoboSuite environment. This data was imported into RoboFlow, where my peers and I carefully annotated each image.

After annotation, YOLO (You Only Look Once) was trained as the object detection model. Its bounding box outputs were then combined with RoboSuite's simulation data, including positional coordinates and quaternion orientation, providing precise localization. This integration ensured accurate tracking of objects in 3D space, laying a strong foundation for the subsequent training of the XYZ and YAW models, critical for the pick-and-place task.
Training the Model: Data to Detection Insights

The XYZ model was developed to predict the precise spatial positioning of objects in the simulation. By combining YOLO's bounding boxes with RoboSuite's positional data, the model generated accurate X, Y, and Z coordinates. These coordinates guided the robot’s end-effector to the correct position for object pickup.
Through extensive testing, the model achieved an accuracy rate of 97%, consistently predicting object positions with minimal error, ensuring reliable performance for the pick-and-place task.

The YAW model was designed to predict the rotational orientation of objects, a critical factor for ensuring the robot could pick up and place items correctly. Using the localized dataset, including YOLO's bounding boxes and quaternion data from RoboSuite, the model accurately predicted the YAW angle, aligning the robot’s gripper to the object’s orientation.
Testing revealed the model achieved an accuracy rate of 83%, enabling reliable alignment and improving the overall precision of the pick-and-place task.

With the trained XYZ and YAW models providing accurate predictions for object position and orientation, PID (Proportional-Integral-Derivative) control was implemented to fine-tune the robot’s movements. This control system adjusted the robot’s speed and position dynamically based on real-time feedback, ensuring smooth and precise alignment with the predicted object coordinates.
PID control minimized errors such as overshooting or instability, significantly enhancing the robot’s ability to pick up and place objects accurately in the simulation.
Precision in Action: Robot Targeting Objects

After integrating all components—object detection, XYZ and YAW models, and PID control—the robot successfully performed the pick-and-place task in the simulation. The video showcases the robot accurately detecting, positioning, and orienting objects before completing the placement process.
My journey through this project provided several key insights.

Combining object detection with XYZ and YAW models created a system for accurate positioning and orientation. This showed how useful it is to integrate different models to solve complex tasks in robotics.
PID control helped improve robotic precision by adjusting movements in real-time, ensuring smooth and accurate pick-and-place actions.
Using open-source models like YOLO sped up the development process. It provided a strong base for object detection, allowing more time to focus on improving other parts of the system.
Simulations allowed testing and refining ideas without risk. However, they also showed that real-world applications could be more challenging, requiring further adjustments and development.
